newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Big bonuses can leave banks exposed to losses.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Big bonuses can leave banks exposed to losses.

text.p: Banks and financial institutions who pay traders according to the profits they make are actively encouraging risk and leave themselves wide open to potentially huge losses, analysts said on Monday.

The trading debacle at Britain's NatWest has again proved that unless rock-solid risk management structures are in place to pick up errors or intentional cover-ups in increasingly complex market instruments, it can be a recipe for disaster.

National Westminster Bank, one of Britain's largest, has had to write off 50 million sterling ($81.2 million) after it found "mispricing errors" by one trader on the interest rate options book of its markets arm.
Analysts said while the vast majority of traders do not take undue risk and are completely honest, it only takes one to cause financial mayhem.

This was proved two years ago when British investment bank Barings collapsed under the weight of some 800 million sterling of losses in unauthorised derivatives trades by Nick Leeson, who is currently languishing in a Singapore jail.

"In effect you are paying people by the amount of risk they are taking," said one analyst. "The more risk they take the more they believe they are going to get paid...and they are not risking their own capital."

The Bank of England recognises the problem and said in its latest Financial Stability Review on Monday that salary and bonus policies of firms in the financial markets were an increasing concern to regulators.
"If large bonuses are paid to employees who make money but are perceived to have a cavalier attitude to compliance, it is likely to encourage similar behaviour in others," the central bank said.
This piece of 'Central Bankspeak' is simply a warning to banks that if a trader plays fast and loose with its money and is seen to get away with it, it could prompt others to do the same.
"The unscrupulous, or inept, are not risking their own capital," said another analyst who also declined to be named.
"If they lose, the worst that can happen is that they are out of a job, but the worst that can happen for the bank is that they lose half their balance sheet."

The fact that this kind of thing happens indicates that there is still a yawning gulf in the understanding of some financial products between the front-line trading operations and the back-office management.
Banks must either beef up their risk management away from the front-line operations and/or scale down some of the risks they are taking, analysts said.
"There are so many ways you can add risk to the balance sheet that a casual glance would not detect," an analyst said.
"The bonus issue is a difficult one because traders have to be encouraged to make profits for the bank. The only answer would seem to be much better risk management."
So will it happen again? Traders and analysts say it is bound to, given the huge size of financial markets, with the foreign exchange market alone turning over more than a trillion dollars a day.
"With markets as big as they are it is bound to happen again," said one foreign exchange trader, who wondered just how many cases of big trading losses through dubious or inept trading go unreported.
"It's so embarrassing for banks -- I wonder how many times this kind of thing happens and they just sack the guy and keep quiet."
